implementation_notes: extend Forwardable followed by def_delegator :@repo, :cancel, :cancel_order defines the intention-revealing one-liner for you (the third argument is the rename), and def_delegators :@repo, :count, :empty? generates several at once without renaming; the documentation describes both as defining delegator instance methods to a designated object. This is the pattern as a standard-library facility, so the classic structure is generated rather than hand-written and the list of forwarded operations lives in one declarative place. Use it when a class forwards a handful of operations to one collaborator; write the method out by hand (or use Ruby 3's endless def) when the body deserves to be visible in the source.
code_sketch:
require "forwardable"

class OrderService
  extend Forwardable
  def_delegator :@repo, :cancel, :cancel_order    # named one-line delegation
  def_delegators :@repo, :count, :empty?          # several at once

  def initialize(repo) = @repo = repo
end
pitfalls: The macros run while the class body is evaluated, so extend Forwardable must appear before any def_delegator call - otherwise the delegating methods never exist.
def_delegators cannot rename, so callers inherit the delegate's vocabulary; only the singular def_delegator :@repo, :cancel, :cancel_order buys an intention-revealing name.
The generated method has no source in your class: source_location points into forwardable.rb and stack traces show the delegator wrapper, which slows down debugging.

variants.name: Endless method definition (Ruby 3.0+)
variants.implementation_notes: Ruby 3.0's endless method definition writes the one-liner in the language itself: def cancel_order(id) = @repo.cancel(id), with def count = @repo.count for the argument-less case. Choose it over Forwardable when the forwarded expression should be visible in the class source, when a class forwards one or two methods rather than a list, or when a code reviewer must see exactly what is delegated; the body is a single expression, so anything that needs rescue, ensure or a second statement must be written as an ordinary method (or left to the stdlib delegator, which also records the forwarding in one place).
variants.code_sketch:
class OrderService
  def initialize(repo) = @repo = repo
  def cancel_order(id) = @repo.cancel(id)
  def count = @repo.count
end
pitfalls: An endless method is a single expression: there is no place for rescue/ensure or a multi-line body, and Ruby 2.x does not parse it at all - a gem that supports older rubies cannot use it.

Endless definitions with parameters require the parenthesized parameter list; dropping the parentheses changes the parse (a bare name after def is read as the method name, not an empty argument list).
